doc.title: Harold Ousley interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Paris trip, Le Chat qui Peche and first Bethlehem recording
summary: Ousley tells of touring with the Festival of Songs show, staying in Paris, working at Le Chat qui Peche with J.T. Hogan and Clark Terry, and recording for Bethlehem.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Whew. So your first recording opportunity —

That was with Bethlehem Records. And this was in ’60. And I’m trying to think, did I — I recorded when I came back from Europe. Because I went to Paris, I was on a show which was more or less like a rock & roll show, “Festival of Songs.” And they had Jay and the Americans.

Jay and the Americans was one of the headlining groups, and I was with a group called Ray Scott, he was a singer, and we had a girl drummer. And the show toured in Italy on the coastline, all of the resorts down the coast line, Viareggio, we even went to Rome. Then after we left there we ended up in France and — oh right now the name escapes me, but it’s one of the places where they have the festivals in the south of France. And after then I think — oh we ended up in Paris, because we played Salle Pleyel, and they gave © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

me a chance to get to Paris. So I left, well the show ended there and I stayed in Paris and I lived over in Montmarte. And I used to take the — well they call it the metro there. So I learned how to use the metro and you’d get all over Paris. And the great thing about the metro, if you knew where you were going you could find it very easily. And so I would go over to the Left Bank. In fact the club I worked in was a club called oh, Le Chat qui Peche, which means a cat with fishes. And the lady who owned the club was Madame Ricard. She used to smoke a cigar all the time. And she was one of the freedom fighters during the war. And where we played was down in the basement. And I think maybe at that time during the war there was maybe like a secret place that they utilized. But this was a cave where the music was. And because when I first came to Paris I heard about, they told me about the Chat qui Peche. And I went over there, a friend of mine, J.T. Hogan, a drummer, was working there. He had a band. And so I sat in and played, and he hired me. And at that time Alice Coltrane, who was not Coltrane then, she was married to a singer, Poncho [Kenny] Hagood, who used to work with Diz. And she was, they were living in Paris. She was a piano player there, and then when Clark Terry came over with Duke to join Free and Easy, which was a show that Quincy Jones had written, and that was a band full of stars man, everybody you can think of was in there. So it was like old home week. Because everybody used to meet. There was a place called Gabby and Haynes. And I forget — Gabby, I think that was a woman, and Haynes was a man. But he was a cook and he was from the United States. And it was a mixed couple. But their cooking, you could get greens, you could get all the home cooking. So everybody used to come there and meet and eat and drink. But it was just great. It was a good time to be there. When Clark joined Free and Easy and left the show, he came to work at the Chat qui Peche. And he and I worked together. And so it was a very good — when I came back, that’s when I did the Bethlehem recording. Because on the cover I had on a French tam and they had the setting like in France. Because over there they had, with the advertisements, they have a sort of cylindrical thing that they put the advertisement on.

So they had this kind of a thing on the cover, but it wasn’t a real thing. I had to pretend like I was learning up against it because if I leaned it would fall over, just a piece of cardboard. But that was because I had just came back. But that was the first recording. I’m sorry to make this so long.
